How to analyze Pakistani bank stocks

Banks are not cement plants. They take deposits, make loans and earn spreads and fees while managing credit risk and capital rules. Use bank-specific lenses before you compare them with industrial companies on a simple P/E.

By PSX Tracker · Updated 23 September 2026

Franchise and funding

A durable deposit base — especially lower-cost deposits — supports lending. Watch deposit growth and mix in investor presentations.

Rapid loan growth without funding quality can be a warning, not a trophy.

Net interest margin and fees

Net interest margin (NIM) reflects earning assets versus funding costs. Rate cycles move NIM; read management commentary for drivers.

Fee income and operating efficiency also shape profits when margins compress.

Asset quality and capital

Non-performing loans, provisioning and capital adequacy show whether earnings are resilient. Credit losses can erase years of apparent progress.

Regulated capital ratios exist for a reason — skimping here is not a free boost to ROE.

Returns and valuation

Investors often watch ROE, dividend patterns and price-to-book alongside earnings multiples. Compare peers across cycles rather than one snapshot.

If you invest, record your lots and dividends so personal results stay measurable in a tool like PSX Tracker.

A bank’s product is a spread and a promise

A commercial bank takes deposits, makes loans and investments, and earns the difference, minus credit losses and operating costs. That difference is not a factory’s gross margin. Comparing a bank’s “P/E” with a cement company’s P/E, as if they were the same kind of cheap, is a category error. Start with the banking figures.

Islamic banks do the same economic job under contracts that are meant to avoid interest. Their reports use different words. The questions — quality of financing, funding stability, capital — still need answers. The halal guide explains why the word “Islamic” on a bank is the start of a reading, not the end of one.

You are buying a leveraged institution. A bank’s equity is a thin layer under a large pool of other people’s money. Small changes in asset quality move the equity hard. That is the reason bank analysis starts with the loan book and the capital, not with the share-price chart.

Deposits and funding

Deposits are the raw material. Current and savings accounts are usually cheaper and stickier than borrowing in the wholesale market. A bank that funds itself expensively will look fine while rates cooperate and strained when they do not. The deposit note and the mix over several years tell you more than one quarter’s profit.

Growth in deposits is only good when the bank can place the money in assets it understands. Deposit growth that races ahead of the bank’s ability to underwrite is how later losses get financed.

Related-party deposits and deposits from government or other concentrated sources deserve a look. Cheap funding that can leave in a season is not the same as a wide branch base of small accounts.

Net interest margin, or its Islamic analogue

The margin measures what the bank earns on assets minus what it pays on funding, relative to the size of the book. It moves with the policy rate, the mix of deposits, and competition for loans. A wide margin in one year can be the rate cycle, not a permanent skill.

Read the margin next to the fee income. Some banks earn a durable share from fees and services. Others lean entirely on the spread. The mix changes how painful a turn in rates will be.

For an Islamic bank, read the profit-sharing and financing income the way you would read the margin: what was earned, on which book, and whether it is repeating. Do not force the conventional label onto a line that the report has defined differently. Use their definition, consistently, across years.

Credit quality and capital

Non-performing loans are the loans that have already gone bad under the regulator’s definition. Provisions are what the bank has set aside. The interesting question is whether the allowances cover the bad book, and whether the next year’s economy looks like the one in which this coverage was enough. A low NPL ratio after a calm period is not a law of nature.

Capital adequacy is the buffer the regulator requires against losses. A bank can earn a high return on equity partly because it runs with less capital. That return is not free. It is the other side of a thinner buffer. Read the capital ratio beside the return, not instead of it.

Price to book compares the market price with the accounting equity per share. A low multiple can mean the market doubts the book: the loans, the subsidiaries, the assets that have not been marked. A high multiple can mean the market believes the franchise earns more than the book suggests. Neither multiple is a conclusion until you have read the credit section.

Using the reports with the tracker

Once a year, when the annual accounts arrive, update a few lines in your own note: deposit growth, margin, NPL ratio, coverage, capital ratio, and price to book, each with the page they came from. You are building a personal time series the screener will not keep honest for you.

Dividends from banks can be regular and can also be constrained by the regulator or by the need to keep capital. Record what was actually paid. Do not capitalize a hoped-for payout into a value estimate without saying you did that.

Nothing on this page is a ranking of Pakistani banks or a suggestion to prefer one symbol. The reports are public, long, and enough. The app can hold the shares and the dividends after you decide. It cannot read the loan book for you.

Common questions

Which figures come up for PSX banks?

Deposits, net interest margin, non-performing loans, capital adequacy, and price relative to book value. Each one needs the notes in the accounts.

Is a low price-to-book automatically cheap?

No. A lower multiple can reflect weaker asset quality or returns. Read the credit book before treating book value as cash you could collect.

Does the tracker replace a bank’s financial statements?

No. Use the published accounts and regulatory filings. The app can help you keep the portfolio record beside that research.
